sources: Günther Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (Routledge, 2001)
meaningOfNames: Named after its founder, Ptolemy I Soter, and the dynasty descended from him; every male ruler took the name Ptolemy.
'Lagid' is from Lagus, the father of Ptolemy I.
longFormInfo: The Macedonian Greek kingdom that ruled Egypt from the partition of Alexander the Great's empire until the Roman annexation in 30 BCE.
Ptolemy governed Egypt as satrap from 323 BCE, after Alexander's death, and took the title of king in 305 BCE, which is conventionally taken as the kingdom's foundation.
After the defeat at Actium, Octavian took Alexandria in August 30 BCE; Cleopatra VII died by suicide and Egypt became a Roman province.

territory: Egypt throughout, with Cyrenaica and Cyprus for most of its history. Under Ptolemy II and III it also held Coele-Syria, much of the southern Anatolian coast and Aegean islands; these were lost to the Seleucids and Rome from the late third century BCE, leaving Egypt and Cyprus by the first century BCE.

judgments.politicalInfluenceInfo: One of the three great Hellenistic kingdoms, a rival of the Seleucids and a partner and then client of Rome.
judgments.culturalContributionInfo: Alexandria's Library and Mouseion made it the intellectual centre of the Greek world; the Rosetta Stone is one of its decrees.
judgments.scientificAdvancementInfo: Royal patronage supported Euclid, Eratosthenes, Herophilus and Ctesibius.
judgments.ethicalLegacyInfo: A Greek elite ruled a largely Egyptian population, with recurring native revolts.
judgments.economicImpactInfo: Egypt's grain made it the richest Hellenistic state; the crown controlled a monetised, heavily taxed economy.
judgments.militaryImpactInfo: Fought six Syrian Wars with the Seleucids, winning at Raphia (217 BCE).
judgments.surpriseOfImpactInfo: Its last ruler, Cleopatra VII, became one of the most famous figures of antiquity.
sources: Günther Hölbl, A History of the Ptolemaic Empire (Routledge, 2001)

significance: It carried Greek rule, language and learning into Egypt for three centuries and made Alexandria the capital of Hellenistic science and scholarship.
legacy: The Library of Alexandria, the Septuagint translation, Euclid's Elements and the decipherment of hieroglyphs through the Rosetta Stone all trace back to the Ptolemaic court.
shortSummary: The Macedonian Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt from 305 BCE until Cleopatra VII's death and the Roman annexation in 30 BCE, with its capital at Alexandria.
longSummary: Founded by Ptolemy I Soter, a general of Alexander the Great, who governed Egypt as satrap from 323 BCE, first from Memphis and then from Alexandria, and became king in 305 BCE.
The early Ptolemies built an empire across the eastern Mediterranean and made Alexandria, with its Library and Mouseion, the leading city of the Greek world.

From the late third century BCE dynastic conflict, with brothers, sisters and sons reigning jointly and against each other, native revolts and Roman power weakened the kingdom; Rome annexed it in 30 BCE after the defeat of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony.
